Consider a directed weighted graph G(V, E), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges. Suppose we use adjacency list to implement the graph. Consider a sequence of |V| operations with each corresponding to a different vertex in V. For the operation for vertex v, the cost is assumed to be the number of outgoing edges from v.  (a) What is the cost of the worst possible single operation in this sequence of operations? (b) What is the average amortized cost of the above sequence of operations based on aggregate analysis?
resposta:
In a directed weighted graph represented by an adjacency list, the cost of processing a vertex v during an operation is simply the number of outgoing edges stored for v. Consequently, the most expensive individual operation will correspond to the vertex that has the largest out‑degree in the graph. When we run one operation for every vertex, the total amount spent across all operations equals the total number of directed edges in the graph.  

* The worst possible single operation cost is the maximum out‑degree among all vertices, denoted Δ⁺ = max_{v∈V} out‑deg(v).  
* The average amortized cost over the |V| operations is the total cost divided by the number of vertices, which is |E| / |V|, i.e., the average out‑degree per vertex.

First, when the intima becomes roughened or torn—by trauma, inflammation, or endothelial damage—it provides a surface for platelets, fibrin, and red blood cells to adhere and aggregate. This interaction rapidly forms a clot that may not fully seal the defect. **And** this clot can extend into the underlying media, turning what was originally a localized clot into a larger, potentially unstable mass.

Second, under certain hemodynamic conditions the flow of blood can rise enough to lift the compromised distal intima, creating a subintimal dissection. In this situation an intimal flap is pulled away from the wall and blocks the downstream lumen. **But** if the elevated pressure forces blood past the weak spot, it can generate a tear that leaves a gap between the remaining wall and the lumen. **Or** the flap may migrate distally, establishing a new occlusion point.

Third, even when the inner and outer coats of the artery remain intact, red cells and fibrin can collect within the muscular layer. Over days to weeks this accumulation builds up as an intramural hematoma. **Yet** the growth is slow, so the lumen may become progressively narrowed before any external sign appears. **So** clinicians must watch for bruising, pain on exertion, or diminished pulses, because early detection can prevent irreversible stenosis.

Additional contributors include altered shear stress at the lesion site, inflammatory cytokine release from damaged tissue, and hormonal influences such as hypertension or a hypercoagulable state, all of which accelerate clot propagation.

Clinically, patients may present with skin lesions, leg cramps, or reduced peripheral pulses. Imaging studies such as duplex ultrasonography or CT angiography help differentiate a clot, a flap, or an internal bleed. Prompt intervention—whether endovascular stenting or surgical repair—aims to restore flow and preserve tissue viability.

pergunta: in SFM, how exactly can understanding body mechanics and physics influence timing in frames? Create stairs by incrementally indenting each new line.
resposta:
## Short answer **Body‑mechanics & physics tell you *how* a human (or a ragdoll) moves, what forces act on him/her, and how long each “phase” lasts.** When you translate those facts into **frame‑by‑frame timing**, you get motions that look natural instead of robotic. Below is a step‑by‑step breakdown of why that matters for *SFM* – especially when you build a staircase by “incrementally indenting” each new line. --- ## 1. What “timing in frames” means in SFM | Concept | What it controls | Typical unit | |---------|------------------|--------------| | **Frame rate** | Number of snapshots per second (default 24 fps, often 30 fps for filmic work). | `FPS` | | **Keyframe spacing** | Distance between two key poses in seconds (or frames). | e.g., 0.25 s ≈ 8 frames @30 fps | | **Easing / interpolation** | How the values change between keyframes (linear, ease‑in, ease‑out, custom splines). | Controls acceleration/deceleration | | **Physics simulation** | Realistic forces (gravity, drag, collisions) applied to rigid bodies. | Continuous, evaluated every render pass | If you ignore the underlying physics, you’ll end up with “stiff” jumps or unnatural pauses. By respecting them you can **choose the exact number of frames** for each sub‑motion (stance, swing, push‑off, landing). --- ## 2. Body mechanics → frame timing ### 2.1 Limb kinematics & stride cadence - **Leg swing arc**: A typical human leg swings forward and backward in roughly **0.2–0.3 s** (≈12–15 frames at 30 fps). - **Foot‑strike interval**: On a regular stair, the time between successive foot contacts is about **0.8–1.0 s**. - **Center‑of‑mass (CoM) trajectory**: During a step the CoM rises ~0.5 m above the ground and falls back. The rise/fall takes ~0.35 s under Earth’s gravity (g≈9.81 m/s²). > **Takeaway:** If you want a believable walk up a flight of stairs, allocate ~0.35 s for the upward swing, ~0.2 s for the forward swing, and ~0.3 s for the downward swing. Those durations become your target frame counts. ### 2.2 Ground‑reaction forces (GRF) - Each foot strike generates an impulse that pushes the body forward. The **impulse** = change in momentum. - In SFM you can approximate GRF by giving the foot a quick “push” at the moment of contact. The resulting forward velocity builds over ~0.15 s, reaching a peak near the toe‑off point. > **Practical tip:** Add a tiny “kick” (keyframe +0.05 s later) right after the foot lands to mimic the push‑off. ### 2.3 Joint limits & stiffness - Shoulders, hips, knees have angular limits (~120° flexion). - If you exceed them, the chain becomes stiff → jerky motion. Keep the timing short enough that the joint never overshoots its limit. --- ## 3. Physics → frame timing ### 3.1 Projectile / falling objects (stairs themselves) - When a block slides down a stair, it accelerates due to gravity: \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\). - For a 0.5 m drop, \(t = \sqrt{2h/g} ≈ 0.32\) s. - If you animate a “platform” appearing on the floor, you can let it fall naturally by enabling **rigid‑body dynamics** and setting initial position & velocity (zero). The physics engine will handle the descent frame‑by‑frame. ### 3.2 Collision & damping - Stairs are made of many small blocks. Their inter‑block contacts dissipate energy (friction). - In SFM you can turn on **“collision response”** and add a low‑friction coefficient for the floor. This makes the descent feel less abrupt. ### 3.3 Air resistance (minimal for slow motion) - Usually negligible at the speeds involved (<1 m/s). Ignore unless you’re doing high‑speed chase scenes. --- ## 4. Putting it together: Building stairs by “incrementally indenting each new line” Imagine you start with a flat floor and add one step at a time, moving the line **downward** and **backward** slightly each iteration. Here’s how physics/body‑mechanics guide the **frame count** for each insertion: | Step | Geometry | Desired vertical offset | Approx. time to reach offset (under free fall) | Keyframe plan (30 fps) | |------|----------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------| | 1 | First riser (height h₁) | Move line down by h₁ | t₁ = √(2h₁/g) ≈ 0.45 s for h₁=0.5 m | • Frame 0: line at y₀
• Frame 20: line at y₀ – h₁ (using linear interpolation)
• Frame 21: slight “snap” (optional) | | 2 | Second riser (height h₂) | Additional h₂ below previous line | t₂ = √(2h₂/g) ≈ 0.33 s for h₂=0.3 m | Same pattern, but start from the previous line’s position. | | … | … | … | … | … | **Why this works** - **Free‑fall approximation** gives a natural “drop” of the line, mimicking a block sliding down. - Because each line is only moved a few centimeters, the total descent time stays well within the human perception threshold (~0.5 s). - Adding a tiny **ease‑in** at the start of each insertion prevents the sudden jump. ### 4.1 Incremental Indentation Steps (pseudo‑code) ```python # Assume 30 fps => 1 frame ≈ 0.033 s steps = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2] # heights of three riser steps for i, h in enumerate(steps): # Start position: current line top edge pos_start = (0, 0) # arbitrary origin # End position: line shifted down by h pos_end = (0, -h) # negative y = down # Linear interpolation over ~0.45 s (17 frames) n_frames = int(0.45 * 30) # 13.5 → round to 14 for frame in range(n_frames+1): # include start and end t = frame / n_frames # 0..1 y = pos_start[1] + (pos_end[1]-pos_start[1]) * t # Write this as a keyframe (or use a constraint) ``` You can automate this in SFM by **creating a constraint** that drives the line’s Y coordinate according to the equation above, letting the physics engine handle the rest. --- ## 5. Quick checklist for realistic SFM stair sequences | ✅ Item | Why it matters | |--------|----------------| | **Set frame rate** (30 fps for filmic, 60 fps for fast action). | Determines granularity of motion. | | **Use ease‑in/out** on the “landing” pose to avoid abrupt stops. | Human feet don’t stop instantly. | | **Add a small “push‑off” impulse** after each foot strike. | Replicates ground‑reaction force. | | **Enable rigid‑body dynamics** for any animated platforms. | Lets gravity pull them down naturally. | | **Limit joint angles** (shoulder, hip, knee) to prevent overshoot. | Keeps motion smooth. | | **Space keyframes** ~0.2–0.3 s apart for leg swings, ~0.8 s for full step cycle. | Matches biological cadence. | | **For incremental lines**, calculate vertical travel time with \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\) and break it into ~10–15 frames. | Gives a believable “slide”. | | **Test with a simple camera** and watch for “jumps” or “stutter”. Adjust interpolation or add extra frames. | Fine‑tunes realism. | --- ## 6. TL;DR – How body mechanics & physics change frame timing 1. **Biomechanics tells you the *duration* of each phase** (stance, swing, push‑off). Convert those durations to frame counts (`duration × FPS`). 2. **Physics tells you the *acceleration* and *force* during those phases** (gravity pulling a block down, impulse from foot strike). Use those forces to decide whether to add a “kick” or let the system run freely. 3. **Incremental indentation** of a stair line is essentially a controlled free‑fall. Compute the required fall time from height, split it into frames, and interpolate linearly (or with ease‑in) to avoid a jarring jump. By marrying the **human motion data** (joint arcs, stride intervals) with the **physical laws** (gravity, impulse), you can program each frame’s position, rotation, and velocity in a way that feels *exactly* like a real person walking up a staircase—no matter how many lines you add one by one. Happy animating!
